title: Guy Lahneman's shoebox instrument; leaving music for tobacco
summary: Rau describes Guy Lahneman's homemade shoebox-and-car-horn instrument and the college quintet on the Gulf Coast. As bandmates turned professional, Rau went into his father's tobacco business and recounts its founding; he would have liked to teach at Tulane.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: I hate to keep skipping around but I get confused on some of these people that you played with. Did you ever know Guy Lahneman? I knew Guy very well, yeah. Who was he?

He played an instrument that he made out of a shoebox and a car horn. And he could play the damn thing like nobody's business. And he would sing too. I mean he had a sort of a voice like Edmond Sushant. It was one of these grating sort of thing. But he knew how to put it over. They had a wonderful sense of rhythm. And that was Guy's instrument. They had a wooden box about that big with a shoehorn. Not a shoehorn. A car bell nailed onto the damn thing. Between the wooden box and the car bell that was Guy made his music. And he was damn good at it too. Guy was one of the, we called ourselves the college quintet when we were playing over on the Gulf Coast. And that came back to town and evolved into different outfits. And that's about the time I got out of it. Because they started playing professionally. I don't think Guy ever played. He was a pretty damn good life insurance man. He was one of the best in town as a matter of fact, as a young man. But some of the boys got mixed up in the thing professionally and they were playing music. And I had this job here. I mean, I was, this was my father's business. And he got tired of me monkeying around. So I got down here in the tobacco business. But that goes back, as I said before, to W.R.A.B., who was in the tobacco business. And this outfit was in trouble financially. An old man, Duke, the original James P. Duke of the tobacco company, American Tobacco Company, sent down to Mr. Irby to see if he couldn't find somebody to take this thing over. So Mr. Irby talked to my father. And my father said, well, he'd give it a try if he could get somebody to handle the sales of him, because he wasn't a salesman. So that's where the DeBens came into the picture. The Chairs DeBens was the father of these boys here. And grandfathers, some of them. And between them, they raised enough money. Mr. DeBens, my father, and his brother raised enough money to float this, get it started. And that was the beginning of the, I think they raised $20,000 between them. And assumed the debts, of course, which it was. But they were then still part of the American Tobacco Company. They hadn't paid up everything yet at that time. And they used to, the American Tobacco Company, put in their bookkeeping system, accounting system. And my father was always very proud of it, because he thought it was way ahead of its time for concern our size. But we used to, I remember his, having to send reports up to New York every month. And, up until the time they paid out their debt, we were still, ostensibly, part of the American Tobacco Company. And, up until the time they got started. It took a little while to get it straightened out, but they did. And that, that's how I happened to be in there, because he was my father and my father was Mr. Irby's secretary. Mr. Irby was the Irby branch of the League of Mine Tobacco Company. So, I'd add it up to the tobacco business instead of me being a musician or a schoolteacher. I would have liked to teach at Tulane. I liked teaching, but there wasn't much money in it, as you can see. I got paid $850 for the whole year.
